section_summaries.epidemiology: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI), prevalent in all sexually active populations, with prevalence highest in younger age groups. The World Health Organization estimates 131 million new cases of genital chlamydial infection occur annually worldwide.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: After an incubation period of 5 to 10 days, C. trachomatis elicits an acute inflammatory response with a purulent exudate. Chronic inflammation then develops, leading to sub-epithelial follicles, fibrosis, and scarring, which cause much of the associated morbidity, especially after repeated infections. Infection is most prevalent in younger, sexually active age groups, suggesting a degree of protective immunity. Cell-mediated immune responses, particularly by CD4+ lymphocytes, are crucial for clearing the infection. Vaccine trials and recombinant antigens have shown some protective effects in animal models.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Genital C. trachomatis infection symptoms are similar to gonorrhea but usually less severe, and many infections are asymptomatic. Long-term sequelae, such as infertility and ectopic pregnancy, result from fibrosis and scarring after prolonged or repeated infections. In men, manifestations include urethritis (dysuria, mucopurulent discharge), epididymitis (scrotal pain, swelling, tenderness, fever), and proctitis. In women, cervicitis (mucopurulent discharge, hypertrophic cervical ectopy), urethritis (urethral syndrome), and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) can occur, potentially leading to infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. It may also be associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes and cervical squamous cell carcinoma. In both sexes, adult paratrachoma (inclusion conjunctivitis) and otitis media can manifest, as can reactive arthritis. Neonatal infections include conjunctivitis and pneumonia.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are the most sensitive and specific diagnostic method, usable with urine samples or self-administered vaginal swabs. Traditional methods like culture, direct immunofluorescence, and enzyme immunoassays are less sensitive. Rapid real-time PCR NAATs, such as the Cepheid GeneXpert, provide quick results. Serologic tests can be helpful for PID, lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, and C. pneumoniae infection, with C. trachomatis IgM antibody being the gold standard for chlamydial pneumonia in babies.
section_summaries.treatment: Uncomplicated C. trachomatis infections are treated with a single 1g dose of azithromycin or 100mg doxycycline twice daily for 7 days; doxycycline is recommended for anorectal infections. Chlamydial PID is treated with 100mg doxycycline twice daily for 14 days. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy, where azithromycin 1g or amoxicillin 500mg three times daily for 7 days are safe and effective. Ofloxacin is active but not widely used. Ophthalmia neonatorum and neonatal pneumonia are treated with erythromycin syrup. For LGV, C. pneumoniae, or C. psittaci, doxycycline 100mg twice daily or erythromycin 500mg four times daily for 21 days is recommended, with macrolides or tetracyclines generally advised for C. pneumoniae and C. psittaci, and prolonged courses for pneumonia.
section_summaries.prevention: There is currently no vaccine against chlamydial infection. Control measures rely on case finding, screening, and prompt treatment of patients and their sexual partners.
